messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 53

He is 50, European, married, and works as a psychologist, a profession that has long given him a sense of steadiness and competence. Before the assault, he thinks of himself as someone who can sit with pain without being overwhelmed by it. He spends his days listening carefully, noticing shifts in posture and tone, helping other people find words for things they have hidden from themselves. He is used to being the calm one. That identity fractures one evening after a professional conference, when he is raped by a man he has met only briefly through the event.

In the first hours afterward, he moves through things as if underwater. He remembers getting home and standing in the bathroom with the light too bright, staring at his own face in the mirror and not fully recognizing it. He showers for a long time, scrubbing hard enough to leave his skin raw, then feels ashamed almost immediately, as if the scrubbing means something about weakness or contamination. He tells no one. Not his wife, not his closest colleague, not the police. What takes shape first is not language but disbelief: this did not happen, or if it did, it does not belong to him. He goes back to work the next morning and conducts his sessions with a strange split inside himself, one part speaking in a familiar professional voice while another part is fixed on flashes of the night before.

Over the next weeks, the memories begin breaking through without warning. A patient mentions feeling trapped, and suddenly he is back in the hotel room, his chest tight, his vision narrowed. He starts avoiding certain kinds of clinical work, especially with male patients who are physically imposing or disclose sexual aggression. He changes routes in the hospital corridor to avoid passing the conference center where follow-up meetings are sometimes held. He tells himself these are practical decisions, but privately he knows his world is shrinking.

At night he sleeps lightly, if at all. He wakes with his heart pounding, sometimes already halfway out of bed before he is fully conscious. In dreams he is voiceless, trying to call out and hearing nothing come. His wife notices first that he startles when she touches his shoulder from behind. Then she notices how often he says he is tired, how often he stays late at his office but comes home having completed very little. He becomes irritable in ways that embarrass him: snapping when she asks an ordinary question, feeling sudden anger at small inconveniences, then retreating into apology without explanation. He cannot bear the tenderness in her face when she asks if something is wrong. Tenderness feels dangerous; it gets too close.

As the months pass, shame settles into him with more force than fear. He finds himself thinking in the same blaming language he has challenged in patients for years. He should have seen it coming. He should have fought harder. He should not have frozen. Because he is a psychologist, he feels an added layer of humiliation, as though knowledge should have protected him. He knows, intellectually, how trauma works in the body. He knows about dissociation, avoidance, hypervigilance, intrusive memory. Yet the knowing does not stop him from checking locks repeatedly at night, from scanning other men’s expressions for threat, from feeling his stomach drop when an unknown number appears on his phone.

His work begins to suffer in subtler ways. He is still reliable, still composed enough that most patients likely do not notice, but he notices. He loses the thread of sessions. At moments he feels emotionally absent, watching himself ask the right questions while feeling nothing. At other moments he is flooded by too much feeling and has to grip the arm of his chair to stay present. Cases involving sexual trauma now leave him rattled for hours. He dreads supervision meetings because he fears a colleague will hear something strained in his voice and ask the one question he cannot yet answer honestly.

At home, his marriage narrows around silence. He loves his wife and feels guilty for shutting her out, but intimacy has become entangled with fear and disgust. When she reaches for him in bed, he tenses before he can stop himself. He starts timing his nights so that he comes to bed after she is asleep. Once, when she touches his chest unexpectedly, he shoves her hand away with such force that both of them go still. He apologizes over and over, but cannot explain the panic behind it. After that, she becomes gentler, more careful, and he hates that too, because it confirms that something fundamental has changed.

Now, many months later, he describes living with a constant internal brace, as though his body is preparing for another blow. He still goes to work, still writes notes, still offers calm interpretations in a room designed to make other people feel safe. But he no longer feels safely inside his own life. He measures distance to doors, notices footsteps in hallways, avoids conferences, avoids hotels, avoids being alone with men he does not know. What troubles him most is not only what happened, but how persistently it remains present. He says the assault did not stay in the past; it follows him into sleep, into marriage, into the consulting room, into the private space where he once felt most sure of who he was.
